title: Lab 5
text:
Why not a linear model?









The DHARMa plots indicate that a linear model is inappropriate for this data. The QQ plot shows that the residuals significantly deviate from the diagonal line. Moreover, the residuals vs-fitted plot should show the red lines flat to the dashed lines. What this data shows, however, is a significant deviation, indicating that this model fails to model the data.
If we are to apply this linear model to the count data we are in danger of distorting the effect sizes and increasing the rate of error, which can lead to incorrect interpretation of the results.
Therefore, we will apply poisson and negative binomial models to this data.

data:  simulationOutput
dispersion = 7.2521, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided










    DHARMa zero-inflation test via comparison to expected zeros with
    simulation under H0 = fitted model

data:  simulationOutput
ratioObsSim = 15.035, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


The DHARMa plots indicate that, like the linear model, the poisson model is inappropriate for this data. The QQ plot shows that the relationship between the predictors and outcome are not linear as the residuals deviate significantly from the line. Moreover, the residuals vs-fitted plot shows that the red lines do not follow the dashed lines.
The dispersion ratio is 7.25 (p < .001) and therefore our standard errors are two small. This indicates that the observed data are significantly more variable than a poisson model expects, which is variance that is equal to the mean. Moreover, there are 15.03 times as many zeros as the Poisson expects. This indicates that the data are over dispersed, and that we should move to a model that accounts for this to avoid misinterpreting a smaller standard error and confidence interval with inflated p-values. We cannot jump straight to a zero inflation model because we do not yet know if the overdispersion itself is causing the extra zeroes so it is best to add a dispersion parameter first.

title: Lab 5
section: Do the zeros need their own model?
text:
Do the zeros need their own model?
The NB’s zero-inflation test showed the model does not reproduce the observed zeros well (observed/expected = 1.1, p = 0). The Negative Binomial model under predicts the zeros, therefore a Zero-Inflated or Hurdle model for zeros is needed.


            df      AIC
neg.binom    8 24469.91
m.zinb       9 24471.19
m.zinb.full 15 24340.77
m.hurd      15 24330.41


            df      BIC
neg.binom    8 24521.03
m.zinb       9 24528.71
m.zinb.full 15 24436.63
m.hurd      15 24426.27









The zero-inflation model with full predictors for zero fit significantly better than the negative binomial model as shown by the likelihood ratio text, χ²(7) = 143.14, p < .001. The model with a constant zero inflation probability had a higher AIC and BIC than the negative binomial model, while the foll zero inflation model was lower than both. Moreover, the Hurdle model has the lowest AIC and BIC out of all the models, but it is not a meaningful difference compared to the full zero inflation model. Therefore the Full zero inflation model will be the chosen model. This choice is solidified by the zero-inflation test, which showed the model reproduces the observed zeros well (observed/expected = 0.96, p = 0.18).

title: Lab 5
text:
11. Results write-up
The number of visits were overdispersed (M = 5.77, s² = 45.69; 16 zeros). Residual checks on the poisson model showed overdispersion (dispersion ratio = 7.25 (p < .001) and excess zeros (observed/expected = 15.03, p = 0). Using a negative binomial model resolved the over dispersion (dispersion ratio = 1.04 (p = 0.43)), but not zeros (observed/expected = 1.1, p = 0). Finally, a zero-inflation model was chosen to account for this (observed/expected = 0.96, p = 0.18).
Holding other predictors constant, each increase in chronic conditions was associated with older adults visiting a physician more times (b = 0.149, p < .001). Poor health compared to average health was associated with an increase in visiting a physician (b = 0.350, p < .001) while excellent health compared to average health was associated with a decrease in the same (b = −0.349, p < .001). Females visited the physician more times than males (b = 0.072, p = .022), as did those who have insurance (b = 0.1528, p < .001). Moreover, greater years of school were associated with visiting the physician more times (b = 0.022, p < .001).
Finally, the interaction between chronic conditions and insurance was not significant here (b = -0.053, p = .052) and the model without the interaction was significantly better in the likelihood ratio test (p = 0).
